entry: Two-humped camel native to the steppes of Central Asia. Its population of 2 million exists mainly in domesticated form. The domesticated Bactrian camel, *Camelus bactrianus*, has served as a pack animal in inner Asia since ancient times, and its tolerance for cold, drought and high altitudes enabled caravans on the [[Silk Road]]. It is the largest living camel, though shorter at the shoulder than the [[Dromedary]]. [[Aristotle]] was the first European to describe camels, in his 4th century BCE *History of Animals*, and [[Carl Linnaeus]] gave the species its current binomial name in 1758. The Bactrian camel and the dromedary often interbreed to produce fertile offspring. Domestic Bactrians do not descend from the wild Bactrian camel (*C. ferus*), the only truly wild camelid in the Old World; the two species split around 1 million years ago.

Puerto Rican rapper, singer and record producer. Dubbed the "King of Latin Trap," he is widely credited with helping Spanish-language rap reach mainstream global popularity. His second solo album, *YHLQMDLG* (2020), became [[Spotify]]'s most-streamed album of the year worldwide. His album *Debí Tirar Más Fotos* (2025) became the first Spanish-language album to win the [[Grammy Awards|Grammy Award]] for Album of the Year. He began appearing on [[WWE]] programming in 2021 and has also appeared in films including *Bullet Train* (2022).

Seventh studio album by American singer [[Michael Jackson]]. Released August 31, 1987, by Epic Records, *Bad* was Jackson's third and final collaboration with producer [[Quincy Jones]]. Jackson composed and co-produced all but two of its tracks, and the dance-pop and R&B album features appearances by Siedah Garrett and [[Stevie Wonder]]. The album produced five number-one singles on the Billboard Hot 100 and remained atop the Billboard Top Pop Albums chart for six consecutive weeks. It has sold over 35 million copies worldwide and is certified 11× platinum in the U.S. It won [[Grammy Awards]] for Best Engineered Recording – Non Classical and Best Music Video ("Leave Me Alone").

Landlocked state in southwestern Germany, east of the Rhine. Its capital is [[Stuttgart]], also the largest city. Formed from the historical territories of Baden, Württemberg and Prussian Hohenzollern, it became a state of [[West Germany]] in April 1952. With more than 11.07 million inhabitants as of 2019 across nearly 35,752 sq km, it is the third-largest German state by area and population. It ranks third among German states by gross regional product and first by exports, research and development spending and patent applications. Companies headquartered there include Mercedes-Benz Group, Porsche, Bosch and SAP.

Medium-sized, short-legged omnivore in the superfamily Musteloidea. Badgers are a polyphyletic grouping, united by squat bodies and adaptations for digging rather than by ancestry. The 15 mustelid badger species are grouped in four subfamilies, including the [[European badger]] and the [[Honey badger|honey badger]], or ratel. Their diet includes rodents, insects, [[Earthworm|earthworms]], roots and fruits. They have short, wide bodies, weasel-like heads and black faces with white markings. They weigh around 9–11 kg, though some Eurasian badgers weigh around 18 kg.

Dry terrain of heavily eroded, softer sedimentary rock and clay-rich soil. It has steep slopes, minimal vegetation, little regolith and a very high drainage density of 48 to 464 km per sq km. Ravines, gullies, buttes and hoodoos are common, and the buttes and hoodoos are capped by resistant sandstone. Badlands occur on every continent except [[Antarctica]], most often where unconsolidated sediments lie. An impermeable, easily eroded surface, sparse vegetation and infrequent heavy rain form them, and overgrazing or pollution can produce anthropogenic badlands. Badlands National Park in [[South Dakota]] erodes at about 25 mm (one inch) per year.

Racquet sport in which a shuttlecock is hit across a net. Played as singles (one player per side) or doubles (two per side), it is often a casual outdoor activity, while professional games use a rectangular indoor court. Shuttlecocks have much higher [[Drag (physics)|drag]] than other balls and decelerate rapidly, yet their high top speed makes badminton the fastest racquet sport in the world. The modern game developed in the mid-19th century among British expatriate officers in [[India]] as a variant of battledore and shuttlecock. Its name derives from the Duke of Beaufort's Badminton House in [[Gloucestershire]], though why or when remains unclear. The first rules were drawn up in [[Pune]] in 1873. Badminton debuted as a Summer Olympic sport in 1992, and mixed doubles was added four years later. Denmark dominated European play, while the game has become very popular in Asia.

Marginal sea of the Arctic Ocean between [[Baffin Island]] and the west coast of [[Greenland]]. It connects to the [[Atlantic Ocean|Atlantic]] through the Davis Strait and the Labrador Sea, and to the Arctic Ocean through the narrower Nares Strait. Ice and icebergs make the bay unnavigable most of the year, though a polynya of about 80,000 sq km, known as the North Water, opens in summer. The area has been inhabited since c. 500 BC, and [[Inuit]] settlements remain on the Canadian coast. English explorer John Davis was the first recorded European to enter the bay, in 1585. The bay is named for William Baffin, who charted its northern reaches in 1616 and held out no hope of an ice-free passage. A magnitude 7.3 earthquake in 1933, the largest known north of the [[Arctic Circle]], had its epicenter here but caused no damage.

Largest island in Canada, in the territory of [[Nunavut]] (pop., 2021: 13,039). It is the second-largest island in the Americas, after [[Greenland]], and the fifth-largest in the world. Iqaluit, Nunavut's capital, lies on Frobisher Bay at the southern tip. The island has been inhabited for at least 3,000 years, and most residents are [[Inuit]]. The climate is polar, with long, cold winters and brief summers. The economy relies on hunting and fishing, supplemented by government services, tourism and limited mining. Wildlife includes [[Polar bear|polar bears]], caribou, seals and narwhals.

Capital and largest city of Iraq, on the [[Tigris]] River. Founded in 762 by the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur, it became the capital of the [[Abbasid Caliphate]] and a center of the [[Islamic Golden Age]]. Its [[House of Wisdom]] and multi-ethnic, multi-religious environment earned it a reputation as the "Center of Learning." During the Abbasid era it was one of the largest cities in the world, with a population above one million. The [[Mongol Empire]] largely destroyed it in 1258, and centuries of decline followed. Baghdad became the capital of Mandatory Iraq during World War I. The [[Iraq War]], which began with the 2003 invasion, caused severe infrastructural damage. Baghdad generates 40% of Iraq's economy and is its seat of government.

Family of [[Woodwind instrument|woodwind]] instruments with enclosed reeds fed from a continuous reservoir of air in a bag. Players blow air into the bag or, on bellows-blown types, squeeze it, keeping a steady airflow while breathing normally. A melodic chanter with finger holes plays the tune, and one or more drone pipes sound sustained tones. Bagpipes have been played for centuries across large parts of [[Europe]], North Africa, West Asia, around the [[Persian Gulf]] and northern [[South Asia]]. The mouth-blown Great Highland bagpipe of [[Scotland]] has three drones, while the bellows-blown Irish uilleann pipes allow seated play. Accounts describe [[Nero|Emperor Nero]] playing a version called the tibia utricularis in the 1st century AD.

Chinese martial art, one of three main *neijia* styles. Its name means "eight trigram palm," referring to the trigrams of the [[I Ching]]. Developed in the mid-19th century during the Qing dynasty, it is widely attributed to Dong Haichuan, who taught in [[Beijing]], though evidence for his invention of it is anecdotal. Training emphasizes circular footwork, circle walking and changing palm techniques. Its fighting approach uses [[Centripetal force|centripetal force]], triangular stepping and open-hand strikes, and it suits encounters with multiple opponents.

Religion founded by [[Baháʼu'lláh]] in the 19th century, teaching the essential worth of all religions and the unity of all people. It developed in Iran and parts of West Asia, where it has faced persecution since its inception. Estimates of its adherents, known as Baháʼís, range from 5 million to 8 million across most of the world's countries and territories. Baháʼís elect local, regional and national administrative bodies, and every five years an election is held for the nine-member Universal House of Justice in [[Haifa]], [[Israel]]. Its teachings hold that a single God reveals religion progressively through Manifestations of God, including [[Jesus]] and [[Muhammad]], and that the major religions are unified in purpose but divergent in practice. The faith rejects racism, sexism and nationalism. Its central figures are the Báb, Baháʼu'lláh and ʻAbdu'l-Bahá.

Iranian religious leader and founder of the [[Baháʼí Faith]]. Born into an aristocratic family, he was exiled from Iran for his adherence to the messianic Bábism, and he was imprisoned in the Síyáh-Chál dungeon before his banishment. In 1863, in Ottoman Iraq, he first announced his claim to a revelation from God. He spent the rest of his life in confinement and exile under the [[Ottoman Empire]], including months in [[Constantinople]], four years of house arrest in Edirne and two years of harsh confinement in Acre. He wrote at least 1,500 letters, translated into at least 802 languages, including *The Hidden Words*, *Kitáb-i-Íqán* and *Kitáb-i-Aqdas*. His burial place near Acre is a pilgrimage destination for Baháʼís.

State in the Northeast Region of Brazil. Its capital, Salvador, was founded in 1549 and served as the first capital of colonial Brazil until 1763. Once dominated by agricultural, slaving and ranching interests, Bahia is now a predominantly working-class industrial and agricultural state. As a primary entry point for enslaved Africans in the [[Atlantic slave trade]], it shaped traditions such as [[Capoeira]]. The state is home to 7% of Brazil's population and produces 4.2% of the country's GDP.

Island country in the eastern Arabian Peninsula, West Asia (pop., 2024: 1,588,670). It comprises 33 natural islands and 50 artificial islands, centered on Bahrain Island, which makes up about 80 percent of its landmass. Manama is its capital and largest city. Bahrain was one of the earliest areas influenced by Islam, during the lifetime of [[Muhammad]] in 628. Portuguese rule from 1521 ended in 1602, when Shah [[Abbas the Great]] of Safavid Iran expelled the Portuguese. The Al Khalifa family has ruled since 1783. Bahrain became a British protectorate in the late 19th century and declared independence in 1971. In 2011, protests inspired by the [[Arab Spring]] occurred, and critics have accused the ruling family of violating the human rights of dissidents and the Shia Muslim population. Bahrain is one of the first post-oil economies in the [[Persian Gulf]] and a member of the [[Arab League]] and the [[United Nations]].

Chinese poet, musician and politician of the [[Tang dynasty]]. Many of his poems concern his career and everyday life, including his time as governor of three provinces. He achieved fame with verse in a plain, near-vernacular style that was popular throughout medieval East Asia, and he composed over 2,800 poems. His long narrative poems include "Song of Everlasting Sorrow," about Yang Guifei, and "Song of the Pipa." In 815 his satirical poems criticizing government mishandling of floods and famines led to his demotion and exile. He later served as prefect of [[Hangzhou]] and [[Suzhou]], and moved his household to [[Luoyang]] in 824. In Japan he is better known as Haku Rakuten, and he was influential in [[Japanese literature]].

Northwesternmost state of Mexico (pop., 2020: 3,769,020). It occupies the northern half of the [[Baja California peninsula]] and covers 70,113 sq km. It was the North Territory of Baja California until it became a state in 1952. Over 75% of its population lives in Mexicali, the capital, Ensenada or [[Tijuana]], the largest city. The Sierra de Baja California includes Picacho del Diablo, the peninsula's highest point, and the Valle de Guadalupe is [[Mexico]]'s major wine-producing area.

Peninsula of northwestern [[Mexico]] between the [[Gulf of California]] and the [[Pacific Ocean]]. It extends 1,247 km from Mexicali in the north to Cabo San Lucas in the south, and its width ranges from 40 km to 320 km. Its area is 143,390 sq km, with about 3,000 km of coastline and approximately 65 islands. The peninsula is separated from mainland Mexico by the Gulf of California and the [[Colorado River]]. Four main deserts occupy it: the San Felipe Desert, the Central Coast Desert, the Vizcaíno Desert and the Magdalena Plain Desert. Its northern half forms the state of [[Baja California]], and its southern half forms Baja California Sur.

First synthetic plastic, a thermosetting phenol formaldehyde resin. [[Leo Baekeland]] developed it in Yonkers, New York, in 1907, and it was patented on December 7, 1909. Its heat resistance and electrical nonconductivity made it useful for insulators and radio and telephone casings. Because it could be molded into any shape, it was also used for kitchenware, jewelry and children's toys. Its commercial success led to other synthetic [[Plastic|plastics]], and the American Chemical Society named it a National Historic Chemical Landmark. Old Bakelite products are now collectible.

City and county seat of Kern County, California, at the southern end of the San Joaquin Valley (pop., 2020: 403,455). Kern County is California's most productive oil-producing county and the fourth most productive agricultural county by value in the U.S. Oil extraction, petroleum refining, food processing and agriculture are major industries. Founded in the late 1860s by Colonel Thomas Baker, it was incorporated in 1873. Bakersfield is the birthplace of the [[Country music|country music]] genre known as the Bakersfield sound.

Method of cooking food with dry heat, usually in an oven, over hot ashes or on hot stones. Heat passes gradually from the surface of unbaked goods to the center, typically at temperatures above 300 °F (148 °C). Dry heat imparts richness through caramelization and surface browning, producing a firm crust and a softer center. Baked goods such as breads, cakes, pastries and cookies rely on [[Flour|flour]] for structure, fats such as butter for tenderness, sugars for sweetness and browning, eggs for binding, and yeast or baking powder for rising. Evidence of leavened bread in [[Ancient Egypt]] dates to around 1500–1300 BCE. Bread and rolls were the most commonly baked foods in 2025. Baking was once done at home and in bakeries, but industrialization automated it in large factories. A person who bakes professionally is called a baker.

Dry chemical leavening agent, a mixture of a carbonate or bicarbonate and a weak acid. A desiccant such as cornstarch keeps the two from reacting prematurely. When dampened, the acid–base reaction releases carbon dioxide, which expands bubbles in batter. Borwick's Baking Powder, launched in England in 1842, was the first commercially sold baking powder. In 1856, Eben Norton Horsford, Rumford Professor at [[Harvard University]], received a patent for a monocalcium phosphate baking powder. In the 1860s he developed the first double-acting baking powder, which releases more gas when heated.

Layered filo pastry dessert filled with chopped nuts and sweetened with syrup or honey. Its origins are debated, and it is traditional across West Asia, Southeast Europe, Central Asia and North Africa. Its precursors trace back to the Assyrian Empire of the 8th century BCE. The modern form emerged around the 15th century in [[Ottoman Empire|Ottoman]] imperial kitchens. The Ottoman Baklava Procession, begun in 1520, carried trays to [[Janissary|Janissary]] soldiers, and the dessert became a symbol of festivity during [[Ramadan]]. Its cultural heritage is disputed between Greece and Turkey.

Capital and largest city of [[Azerbaijan]], on the southern shore of the Absheron Peninsula. Baku is the largest city on the [[Caspian Sea]] and in the [[Caucasus]] region. It lies 28 m (92 ft) below sea level, the lowest-lying national capital in the world. About 25% of Azerbaijan's inhabitants live in its metropolitan area. The first mechanically drilled oil well was established in 1846, and by 1901 Baku was supplying over half of the world's oil. Its Old City, with the Palace of the Shirvanshahs and the Maiden Tower, was designated a [[UNESCO]] World Heritage Site in 2000. Baku hosted the 57th Eurovision Song Contest in 2012 and the 2024 United Nations Climate Change Conference. The city is nicknamed the "City of Winds" for its harsh winds.
